Home

SK-RAFT is an EDA software tool for fault injection in AMD-Xilinx FPGAs. It emulates single-event upsets (SEUs).

This repository contains open-source getting-started examples for the SK-RAFT server. The SK-RAFT server is proprietary SolidKosmos software and requires a valid trial or commercial licence.

Request Free Trial: https://solidkosmos.gr/#try.

Main functions¶

  • Injection into the configuration RAM (CRAM). The CRAM contains the FPGA configuration: CLBs, DSPs, clock managers, IOBs, and all other configurable resources. SK-RAFT can inject faults into all of the CRAM.
  • Injection into the application RAM (ARAM). The ARAM contains the design data during operation: the contents of the BRAMs, the flip-flops, and the LUTRAM.
  • Targeted fault injection. SK-RAFT can limit the injection to:
  • The essential bits of the design.
  • The essential bits of a specific Pblock.
  • The application memories of selected components in your RTL hierarchy.
  • Essential-bit analysis. SK-RAFT reads the Vivado-generated EBD file and finds the essential bits of the design or specific Pblocks.
  • Full BSCAN support. Your script can write inputs to the design and read outputs from the design through the BSCAN user registers (USER1 to USER4).
  • External scrubbing through JTAG. SK-RAFT can scrub the CRAM from outside the FPGA, through JTAG. This function helps during radiation tests.
  • Programmer. SK-RAFT can program the FPGA with a bitstream.
  • XADC and System Monitor access. SK-RAFT can read the temperature and voltage sensors of the XADC (7 series) and of the System Monitor (UltraScale, UltraScale+) through JTAG. It can also set and clear their alarms.
  • TLS connection. The client can connect to the SK-RAFT server through TLS, with the certificates of the server and of the client.
  • Readback with GCAPTURE. SK-RAFT can read back the FPGA's configuration frames. With GCAPTURE, the readback also contains the current values of the flip-flops.

How SK-RAFT operates¶

SK-RAFT is a server:

  • On one side, the server connects to the AMD-Xilinx FPGA through FTDI JTAG (a USB JTAG cable).
  • On the other side, the server receives gRPC requests from clients through TCP/IP.

To inject a fault, your script sends a gRPC request to the server. The server does the operation on the FPGA through JTAG. Then the server sends the result back to your script. The server and your script can be on the same computer (127.0.0.1) or on different computers.

The skraft Python client in this repository sends the gRPC requests for you. A typical script does these steps:

  1. Connect to the server: SkraftFpga.connect(ip, port).
  2. Reserve the board with its serial number: client.attach(serial_number). To find the serial numbers of the connected boards, use client.get_devices().
  3. Upload the design files (bitstream, EBD, LL and XDC files) to the server: dev.uploadDesignToServer(design).
  4. Program the FPGA with an uploaded design: dev.programFPGA(design). The server keeps each uploaded design. Thus, you can upload several designs, and then program the one to use.
  5. Inject faults, for example: dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM).
  6. Read the effect of the faults, for example through BSCAN: dev.read_bscan(...).

Example:

from skraft import Design, SkraftFpga, TargetMemory

with SkraftFpga.connect(ip="127.0.0.1", port=50051) as client:
    with client.attach("210183BFD452A") as dev:
        design = Design(bit="top.bit", ebd="top.ebd")
        dev.uploadDesignToServer(design)
        dev.programFPGA(design)
        report = dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM)
        print(f"far {report.far:#010x} word {report.word_index} bit {report.bit_index}")

Before you inject into the application memory (flip-flops, LUTRAM, BRAM), read the setup rules in docs/general_guidelines.md. For the concepts, refer to docs/concepts.md. For code snippets of the common routines, refer to docs/cheatsheet.md.

Quick start¶

  1. Install the SK-RAFT server with its licence. Connect the FPGA board to the server computer through its USB JTAG cable.
  2. Start the server. On Windows, run the launcher in the bin folder of the server installation:
bin\sk-raft.bat

On Linux, run the server executable of the installation. It takes the same options as on Windows.

The server is ready when it prints:

 ================================================================
 SK-RAFT - Reliability Assessment Fault-emulation Toolkit
 Server 1.x.x (build ef71872, 2026-11-06T13:03:58Z)
 Copyright (c) 2026 SolidKosmos. All rights reserved.
 Use is subject to the SK-RAFT End User License Agreement.
 ----------------------------------------------------------------
 SK-RAFT licence: FULL (Dinkey dongle XXXXXXXXXX)
   Features: application memory injections, pblock injections
 ----------------------------------------------------------------
 Host       windows/amd64, go1.27.3, PID XXXXX
 Log file   C:\path\to\skraft.log
 Designs    C:\path\to\designs
 Listening  [::]:50051, TLS false, client key false
 ================================================================

Keep the server running while you use it. The server serves one client at a time. Another client that connects in the meantime gets the error the server serves only one client and another client is connected.

Option Description
-port <number> The TCP port of the server. The default is 50051.
-tls-cert <file>, -tls-key <file> The TLS certificate and private key (PEM) of the server. With them, the server accepts only TLS connections.
-tls-public-key <file> The public key (or certificate) of the clients that the server accepts. Refer to application_examples/tls_program.

bin\sk-raft.bat -v prints the version of the server. On Windows, the launcher runs the server in %LOCALAPPDATA%\SolidKosmos\sk-raft. The server writes its log, skraft.log, and its cache there. 3. Install the skraft Python client. Refer to Installation. 4. Find the serial number of your board:

python get_started/list_devices.py

The script prints the serial number and the part number of each board that is connected to the server. For a server on another computer, set SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP at the top of the script to the address of that computer. In your own scripts, client.get_devices() gives the same list. 5. Run an example. Start with get_started. It has prebuilt design files for the Basys 3 and the ZedBoard. Set SERIAL_NUMBER and BOARD at the top of the main.py of the example.

Folder structure¶

sk-raft-client/
├── api/python/                           Python client (skraft package) and offline bundle
├── application_examples/                 Example designs and scripts for specific use cases
├── auxiliary_components/                 Reusable BSCAN registers, safe clock, BRAM hold pass
├── docs/                                 Concepts, reference documents and documentation builder
└── get_started/                          Example designs and scripts

Installation¶

The skraft Python client is not on PyPI. Install it from this repository into the virtual environment of your project:

cd your-project
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows
pip install /path/to/api/python

To use local changes to the client without a new installation, use pip install -e /path/to/api/python.

Installation without internet access¶

See ./api/python/offline_bundle

Compatibility¶

The client and the SK-RAFT server have separate versions. The table gives the server versions that the current client supports:

Client (skraft) Supported SK-RAFT server versions
1.0.0 1.0.0
  • The version of the client: pip show skraft.
  • The version of the server: bin\sk-raft.bat -v, or client.version() from a script.

The changes of each version are in CHANGELOG.md.

Documentation¶

To read all the documents of this repository, and the API reference of the client, in a web browser, build the documentation:

docs/html-gen/build_docs.sh      # docs\html-gen\build_docs.bat on Windows

The script writes one HTML file, api/python/dist/skraft-docs-<version>.html. The file contains all the pages, the images and a search. It needs no other file and no internet. Open it in a web browser, or send it to another person.

On the first run, the script creates a virtual environment in docs/html-gen/.venv and installs the packages of docs/html-gen/requirements-docs.txt. This needs internet access and Python 3.11 or later.

Report a problem¶

To report a bug in the client, the examples or the documents, open an issue in the Issues tab of this repository. Use the "Bug report" template. For more information, refer to CONTRIBUTING.md.

SolidKosmos does not accept pull requests from persons outside SolidKosmos.

SK-RAFT getting-started examples¶

Layout¶

get_started/
├── example1/ .. example5/               SK-RAFT client examples (src/main.py)
├── list_devices.py                      lists the boards connected to the server
└── hw/                                  Vivado project (create_project.tcl)
    ├── design_examples/                 design files: design_examples.zip and build output
    ├── sources_1/new/                   VHDL sources
    └── xdc/                             basys3/, zedboard/, custom_template/

Examples¶

# Example Design Purpose
1 example1 targeted_top (fast and slow heartbeat counters, each in its own pblock) Showing how to perform fault injection (FI) into random CRAM bits, random essential CRAM bits, and targeted FI into a Pblock.
2 example2 bscan_adder_top (simplex adder and TMR adder, each in its own pblock. Input and output are provided via BSCAN) Showing how to set up and control a design during fault campaigns through BSCAN.
3 example3 ff_lut_top (flip-flop shift register and LUTRAM) Showing how to inject faults into the ARAM layer, e.g., flip-flop and LUTRAM contents.
4 example4 brams_top (one BRAM with a Hamming SEC code for each byte), and bram_readback_writeback_top in readback_writeback/ (one BRAM with the built-in ECC, no output register) Showing how to inject faults into the BRAMs: You corrupt CRAM bits and content data (ARAM). readback_writeback/ shows what the BRAM outputs during and after an injection into its content: a wrong word while the clock is stopped, then the flipped bit with no ECC error.
5 example5 targeted_top (the design of example 1: the two heartbeats are components of the design hierarchy) Showing how to list the components of a design as a tree, from the flip-flop nets of the LL file, and how to perform random fault injection into the flip-flops of one component, with the net of each flip-flop that an upset hits.

Each example operates with one design. The README of each example shows how to create the files that the SK-RAFT client script uploads to the SK-RAFT server for testing. These files are the bitstream and the EBD, LL and XDC files where necessary. Vivado builds these files from the sources_1/new/*.vhd files of that design in hw.

Requirements¶

  • Tested with Vivado 2025.2.
  • Python 3.9 or a later version, with the skraft package installed (api/python).
  • SK-RAFT server
  • Target FPGA board connected via JTAG to the SK-RAFT server.
  • The design files are listed in each example's README. The script uploads these files to the server.

Prebuilt design files¶

SolidKosmos supplies prebuilt design files for the Basys 3 (basys3) and the ZedBoard (zedboard) in hw/design_examples/design_examples.zip. To extract them, run the script for your operating system:

cd hw/design_examples
./unzip_designs.sh        # Linux
.\unzip_designs.bat       # Windows

The script extracts the bitstream and the EBD, LL and XDC files of each design to hw/design_examples/<board>/<top>/. Then set BOARD in the main.py of the example to your board.

For all other boards, build the design as described below.

Build a design¶

The script create_project.tcl (in hw/) does the full build, from synthesis to bitstream. Then it copies the results to the folder where the main.py of that example expects them. You can run the example immediately after the build.

cd hw
vivado -mode batch -source create_project.tcl -tclargs <device> <top>

<device> selects the board. <top> selects the example:

<top> Example
targeted_top example1, example5
bscan_adder_top example2
ff_lut_top example3
brams_top example4
bram_readback_writeback_top example4 (readback_writeback/)

SolidKosmos tested and supplies only basys3 and zedboard as <device>. To add your own board, refer to "Build a bitstream" in hw/README.md. That section tells you how to:

  1. Copy xdc/custom_template/.
  2. Write the pins of your board.
  3. Add your board to device_info.
  4. Run the build command.

To open the project in the Vivado GUI after the build, add -gui at any position in the arguments. Vivado then stays open. For example:

vivado -mode batch -source create_project.tcl -tclargs zedboard brams_top -gui

After a successful build, the script copies the bitstream, the EBD file, the LL file and board.xdc into hw/design_examples/<device>/<top>/. If this folder does not exist (for example, for your own board), the script creates it. You do not have to copy files manually.

BRAM hold register pass (brams_top)¶

For brams_top, the build runs the BRAM hold register pass before opt_design. The pass is in auxiliary_components/bram_hold_pass.

An SK-RAFT access to BRAM content frames (readback, inject, revert) overwrites the output latch of the block RAMs without an output register. The stored content does not change, but the design would read the overwritten value after the clock resumes. The pass adds a hold register (a flip-flop on the opposite clock edge) behind each BRAM output in use, so the design keeps the word it read before the freeze.

The build prints the report of the pass, and also writes it to bram_hold_pass.rpt in the impl_1 run directory. For brams_top, the report shows the read port of stock_bram as held. The other tops have no block RAM, so the build does not run the pass for them.

The prebuilt brams_top files in design_examples.zip were built with the pass.

Run an example¶

cd exampleN/src
python main.py

The examples do not use command-line options. To configure an example, change the constants at the top of its main.py: SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP, SERIAL_NUMBER, BOARD and the other constants of that example. Then run the script. To find the serial number of your board, run python list_devices.py in this folder.

Each example ends with exit code 0 when it is done, 1 on an error and 130 after Ctrl+C.

Examples 1 to 5 inject faults until you press Enter. Then the example continues to its next step, or it stops. The readback_writeback script of example 4 injects one fault and runs without input.

Examples 1 and 2 correct each upset. Examples 3, 4 and 5 program the FPGA again at the end.

Each example programs the FPGA at the start. Thus you can run the examples in any order, also after you stop one with Ctrl+C. If you write your own script, program the FPGA first.

Example 1: CRAM injection in three steps¶

This example shows the CRAM injection functions of SK-RAFT in three steps on one design. Each step is more selective than the step before it:

  1. Full-device CRAM. The script reads back all the CRAM frames. Then it upsets random bits in these frames.
  2. Essential bits. The server selects each bit from the design's essential bits. The server reads the essential bits from the EBD file.
  3. The essential bits of one pblock. This step is the same as step 2, but in one pblock at a time: first pblock_slow_heartbeat, then pblock_fast_heartbeat.

The script keeps each upset for 100 ms, then flips the same bit again to correct it. Each step, and each pblock in step 3, continues until you press Enter. The script reprograms the FPGA before steps 2 and 3. Monitor the LEDs on the board to see the effect of each upset.

Design¶

The design for this example is targeted_top. It has a fast heartbeat counter and a slow heartbeat counter, each in its own pblock. The XDC file of the design declares the two pblocks, for example:

create_pblock pblock_fast_heartbeat
add_cells_to_pblock [get_pblocks pblock_fast_heartbeat] [get_cells fast_hb_inst]
resize_pblock [get_pblocks pblock_fast_heartbeat] -add {SLICE_X54Y91:SLICE_X57Y99}

A pblock keeps the cells of its instance in the given area. Two more properties control the pblock:

  • set_property EXCLUDE_PLACEMENT true [get_pblocks ...] prevents the placement of other cells in the pblock.
  • set_property CONTAIN_ROUTING true [get_pblocks ...] keeps the routing of the pblock inside the pblock.

The examples do not use CONTAIN_ROUTING, to keep them simple.

The calls of the example¶

Call Use in the example
SkraftFpga.connect(ip=..., port=...), client.attach(SERIAL_NUMBER) Connect to the SK-RAFT server and attach to the device, in with statements that release the device and close the connection.
Design(bit, ebd, xdc), dev.uploadDesignToServer(design), dev.programFPGA(design) Give the design files, upload them to the server and program the FPGA.
dev.configure_seed(0) Set the seed of the random injections. The same seed gives the same upsets in each run.
dev.readback(ReadbackOption.READBACK) Step 1: read back all the CRAM frames. The script selects a random bit of these frames.
dev.inject_at(far, word, bit, TargetMemory.CRAM) Step 1: flip the selected bit. In all steps: flip the bit again after 100 ms, to correct the upset.
dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM), dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock=pblock) Steps 2 and 3: get the number of essential bits of the device, and of each pblock.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM) Step 2: inject one upset into a random essential bit.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock=pblock) Step 3: inject one upset into a random essential bit of one pblock.

Run the example¶

  1. Make sure that the design files are in hw/design_examples/<board>/targeted_top/, and set BOARD in src/main.py to your board. Refer to Build a design or Prebuilt design files.
  2. At the top of src/main.py, set SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP and SERIAL_NUMBER.
  3. Run the script:
cd src
python main.py
Constant Default Description
design targeted_top.{bit,ebd} + XDC The design files. The script uploads them to the server.
SERIAL_NUMBER "210183BFD452A" The serial number of the target board. get_devices() gives the connected boards.
pblocks (in main()) slow and fast heartbeat The pblocks for step 3, as the XDC file names them.

Result¶

Sample output of a run on a Basys 3 (shortened). The frame addresses, the bit counts and the error counts depend on the board, the build and the seed.

programmed 210183BFD452A with ../../hw/design_examples/basys3/targeted_top/targeted_top.bit

Step 1: random bits, anywhere. Press Enter to move on.
frames read back: 5568
  1: far 0x00c000cb word  14 bit  1
  2: far 0x00020a14 word  31 bit 14
...

Step 2: essential bits only (18563) . Press Enter to move on.
  1: far 0x00001400 word  50 bit 31
  2: far 0x0000110d word  87 bit 27
...

Step 3: one pblock at a time.

pblock_slow_heartbeat: essential bits (7166). Press Enter to move on.
  1: far 0x00001423 word  20 bit  4
...

pblock_fast_heartbeat: essential bits (6740). Press Enter to move on.
  1: far 0x00001214 word  86 bit 26
...

Example 1 done.

The script corrects each upset. Thus, the device configuration is clean at the end. If you stop the script with Ctrl+C during an upset, the upset can remain in the device. In that case, reprogram the FPGA before you do any other work.

Example 2: BSCAN-controlled adders, simplex against TMR, single-bit upsets¶

This example programs a bitstream. Then it compares a simplex adder with a triplicated (TMR) adder. Each adder is in its own pblock.

The two adders use one operand register (USER1). Each adder has its own result register: USER2 for the simplex adder and USER3 for the TMR adder.

Each trial does these steps:

  1. It injects one random essential bit into each pblock.
  2. It sends 100 random operand pairs through the two adders.
  3. It marks an adder as failed if one or more of its results are wrong.
  4. It flips the two bits again to correct the upsets.

The trials continue until you press Enter.

The calls of the example¶

Call Use in the example
SkraftFpga.connect(ip=..., port=...), client.attach(SERIAL_NUMBER) Connect to the SK-RAFT server and attach to the device, in with statements that release the device and close the connection.
Design(bit, ebd, xdc), dev.uploadDesignToServer(design), dev.programFPGA(design) Give the design files, upload them to the server and program the FPGA.
dev.configure_seed(0) Set the seed of the random injections. The same seed gives the same upsets in each run.
BscanPrimitive(user, length), dev.write_bscan(primitive, value), dev.read_bscan(primitive) Write the operands through USER1, and read the results of the simplex adder (USER2) and of the TMR adder (USER3).
dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock=...) Get the number of essential bits of each adder pblock.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock=...) Inject one upset into a random essential bit of each adder pblock.
dev.inject_at(far, word, bit, TargetMemory.CRAM) Flip the two bits again after the trial, to correct the upsets.

Run the example¶

  1. Make sure that the design files are in hw/design_examples/<board>/bscan_adder_top/, and set BOARD in src/main.py to your board. Refer to Build a design or Prebuilt design files.
  2. At the top of src/main.py, set SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP and SERIAL_NUMBER.
  3. Run the script:
cd src
python main.py
Constant Default Description
design bscan_adder_top.{bit,ebd} + XDC The design files. The script uploads them to the server.
PBLOCK_SIMPLEX / PBLOCK_TMR "pblock_sngl_add" / "pblock_tmr_add" The two pblocks for the test, as the XDC file names them.
OP_LEN 4 The operand width. It must be equal to the op_len generic of the design.

Result¶

Sample output of a run on a Basys 3 (shortened). The frame addresses, the bit counts and the error counts depend on the board, the build and the seed.

Programmed 210183BFD452A.
Number of Essential Bits in:
Simplex Adder = 595 | TMR Adder = 3374
Press Enter to move on.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Vulnerability Factor (VF) = observable errors / injected faults
# of trials = 156  ||  Simplex Correct VF = 66/156 (42.31%)  |  TMR Correct VF = 5/156 (3.21%)
66 simplex, 5 tmr errors in 156 trials.
Final Simplex Adder VF = 66/156 (42.31%)
Final TMR Adder VF     = 5/156 (3.21%)
Example 2 done.

First, the script prints the number of essential bits in each pblock. Then it updates one status line during the trials. The status line shows:

  • The number of trials.
  • The result of each adder for the last trial: green "Correct" or red "Wrong".
  • The vulnerability factor (VF) of each adder: the fraction of trials in which the adder failed.

When you stop the script, it prints the final error counts and the VFs.

Each trial corrects its bits immediately after the check. Thus the configuration of the device is clean at the end. If you stop the script with Ctrl+C during a trial, a bit can stay flipped. In that case, program the FPGA again before you do other work.

Example 3: Flip-flop shift register and LUTRAM injection¶

This example does two campaigns on one design through BSCAN:

  • Part 1: a shift register with a feedback loop, made of flip-flops.
  • Part 2: a distributed RAM (LUTRAM).

USER1 starts and stops the clock of the shift register and of the LUTRAM. The script reads the shift register through USER2. USER3 and USER4 give access to the LUTRAM (address and data).

Part 1: flip-flops¶

Part 1 injects faults into the flip-flops inside the shift-register's pblock area (pblock_ff_sr_inst) (TargetMemory.FF). The server finds the flip-flops from the LL file. If the pblock contains no flip-flops, the script stops.

Each trial does these steps:

  1. It lets the clock operate for 2 s, and then it stops the clock.
  2. It reads the shift register.
  3. It upsets one flip-flop.
  4. It reads the shift register again and prints the two values.
  5. It starts the clock again.

The script does not correct the upsets. Part 1 continues until you press Enter.

Part 2: LUTRAM¶

Part 2 injects faults into the LUTRAM in pblock_LUTRAM (TargetMemory.LUTRAM). The script does these steps:

  1. With the clock on, it writes a known pattern into each word. Then it reads back each word to make sure that the pattern is correct.
  2. It stops the clock and injects one upset each 0.5 s, until you press Enter.
  3. It starts the clock again and reads back the full array.
  4. It prints each word with the positions of its incorrect bits.

The calls of the example¶

Call Use in the example
SkraftFpga.connect(ip=..., port=...), client.attach(SERIAL_NUMBER) Connect to the SK-RAFT server and attach to the device, in with statements that release the device and close the connection.
Design(bit, ll, xdc), dev.uploadDesignToServer(design), dev.programFPGA(design) Give the design files, upload them to the server and program the FPGA.
dev.configure_seed(0) Set the seed of the random injections. The same seed gives the same upsets in each run.
BscanPrimitive(user, length), dev.write_bscan(primitive, value), dev.read_bscan(primitive) Start and stop the clock (USER1), read the shift register (USER2), and select, write and read a LUTRAM word (USER3, USER4).
dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.FF, pblock=PBLOCK_SR), dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.LUTRAM, pblock=PBLOCK_LUTRAM) Get the number of flip-flop bits and LUTRAM bits of each pblock.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.FF, pblock=PBLOCK_SR) Part 1: inject one upset into a random flip-flop of the shift register.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.LUTRAM, pblock=PBLOCK_LUTRAM) Part 2: inject one upset into a random bit of the LUTRAM.

Run the example¶

  1. Make sure that the design files are in hw/design_examples/<board>/ff_lut_top/, and set BOARD in src/main.py to your board. Refer to Build a design or Prebuilt design files.

The script runs part 1, programs the FPGA again, and runs part 2. Then it programs the FPGA one more time, to make sure that the configuration is clean.

If you stop the script with Ctrl+C during a campaign, the configuration of the device can stay incorrect. In that case, program the FPGA again before you do other work.

Example 4: BRAM injection, configuration bits, content and ECC recovery¶

The design uses one RAMB36 in the 1K x 36 configuration. Each 36-bit word contains 24 data bits and 12 check bits. Logic in the fabric around the BRAM protects each data byte with its own Hamming SEC code (4 check bits for each byte). This logic is not the built-in ECC of the BRAM.

Sequence¶

  1. The script fills the memory. Then it reads back each word to make sure that the data is correct.
  2. Part 1. The script injects essential CRAM upsets (TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM) into the block type 0 frames of the BRAM column. Then it reads back the memory.
  3. The script programs the FPGA again. Thus the upsets of part 1 do not have an effect on part 2.
  4. The script fills the memory again.
  5. Part 2. The script injects content upsets (TargetMemory.BRAM) into the block type 1 frames. The upsets add up, and the script does not correct them.
  6. The script reads back the full memory two times: first with ECC off, then with ECC on.
  7. The script programs the FPGA again, to clear the upsets of part 2.

In the two parts, the script injects one upset each 0.3 s until you press Enter. When part 2 continues for a longer time, more bytes get two or more flips. The SEC code cannot correct these bytes.

BRAM output latch and the hold register¶

When SK-RAFT reads or writes BRAM content frames (part 2 injects into them), the output latch of stock_bram takes a value from the configuration frame. The content of the BRAM does not change. The BRAM has no output register (DO_REG = 0), so without protection the design can take that wrong value instead of the word it read before the freeze.

hw/create_project.tcl builds brams_top with the BRAM hold register pass (auxiliary_components/bram_hold_pass). The pass adds a falling-edge register behind the BRAM output, which keeps the word read before the freeze. Thus a wrong word in the results comes from the injected content, not from the latch. The build prints the report of the pass.

readback_writeback/ shows the effect without the pass, on a BRAM with the built-in ECC: the wrong word while the clock is stopped, and the flipped bit that the ECC does not detect.

BSCAN register map¶

Register Width Access Contents
USER1 1 bit write BRAM clock enable (the script stops the clock during each injection)
USER2 16 bits write Address select (only the low 10 bits have an effect)
USER3 24 bits read/write (check auxiliary_components/bscan/bscan_user_register_io.vhd to see how reads are performed) The data at the selected address
USER4 1 bit write ECC correction enable. It applies to the BRAM read path only. The reset value is 0.

The calls of the example¶

Call Use in the example
SkraftFpga.connect(ip=..., port=...), client.attach(SERIAL_NUMBER) Connect to the SK-RAFT server and attach to the device, in with statements that release the device and close the connection.
Design(bit, ebd, ll, xdc), dev.uploadDesignToServer(design), dev.programFPGA(design) Give the design files, upload them to the server and program the FPGA.
dev.configure_seed(0) Set the seed of the random injections. The same seed gives the same upsets in each run.
BscanPrimitive(user, length), dev.write_bscan(primitive, value), dev.read_bscan(primitive) Start and stop the clock (USER1), select the address (USER2), write and read the data (USER3), and enable the ECC correction (USER4).
dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock=PBLOCK_BRAM), dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.BRAM, pblock=PBLOCK_BRAM) Get the number of essential CRAM bits and of content bits of the BRAM pblock.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock=PBLOCK_BRAM) Part 1: inject one upset into a random essential bit of the BRAM pblock.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.BRAM, pblock=PBLOCK_BRAM) Part 2: inject one upset into a random content bit of the BRAM.
dev.decode_far(far) Get the block type of the frame of each upset (0: configuration, 1: BRAM content).

If the first write and read-back pass finds incorrect data, the script stops. It does not inject faults in that case.

After each read-back, the script prints each incorrect word with these data:

  • The expected data bits.
  • The data bits that it read.
  • The positions of the incorrect bits.

The main result is the number of incorrect addresses with ECC off and with ECC on:

  • A word that is incorrect only with ECC off had single flips. The SEC code corrected them.
  • A word that is incorrect with ECC on had two or more flips in one byte. The SEC code cannot correct these flips, and it can also make an incorrect correction.
  • A flip in a check bit does not show with ECC off. With ECC on, the SEC code hides a single flip in a check bit.

The script does not correct the faults. At the end, it programs the FPGA again to clear them.

Example 4, readback and writeback: a BRAM with built-in ECC under SK-RAFT injection¶

This part of example 4 shows two effects of an SK-RAFT injection into the content of a block RAM that uses the built-in ECC of the BRAM and has no output register (DO_REG = 0):

  1. The configuration access overwrites the output latch of the BRAM. While the clock is stopped, the BRAM outputs a wrong word.
  2. When the clock starts, the BRAM reads the word again. The word has the injected bit flipped, and the ECC does not detect it (SBITERR = 0).

Design¶

bram_readback_writeback_top (hw/sources_1/new/bram_readback_writeback_top.vhd) has one RAMB36 in simple dual-port mode, 512 x 72 (64 data bits and 8 ECC bits). The built-in ECC encoder makes the ECC bits on each write (EN_ECC_WRITE = TRUE). The built-in decoder checks each read (EN_ECC_READ = TRUE). The read port is always enabled, so the BRAM reads the word at the address on each clock edge. The BRAM outputs go directly to USER3, with no register in between.

Register Width Access Contents
USER1 1 bit write Clock enable of the BRAM (a BUFGCE). 0 after programming.
USER2 16 bits write Address (only the low 9 bits have an effect).
USER3 80 bits write Bits 63:0 are written to the word at the address.
USER3 80 bits read Bits 63:0: data. Bits 71:64: ECC parity. Bit 72: SBITERR.

The XDC excludes the BRAM from power optimization (set_power_opt -exclude_cells). Without it, opt_design gates the read enable, and the BRAM does not read again in stage 4.

Stages¶

The script writes the address as the word: word 0 holds 0, word 1 holds 1, and so on. The script reads word 0 after each stage.

Stage Action Result
1 Start the clock, fill the BRAM, select word 0. The word is correct, SBITERR = 0.
2 Stop the clock. The word is still correct. The output latch holds the last read.
3 Inject into word 0, bit 0 (Ram=B:BIT0 in the LL file). The clock is still stopped. A wrong word.
4 Start the clock. Bit 0 is flipped, SBITERR = 0.

Stage 3. To flip one bit, SK-RAFT reads the content frame, changes the bit and writes the frame back. This access to a content frame overwrites the output latch of the BRAM port. The BRAM has no output register, so its outputs show the latch directly: data, parity and SBITERR are not the values of word 0. The same occurs for each readback and each revert of a content frame.

Stage 4. The BRAM reads word 0 again, and the outputs are correct for the stored word. But the frame write went through the ECC encoder of the BRAM, which made new ECC bits for the flipped data. Thus the stored word is a valid ECC word, and the decoder finds no error. The flipped bit is silent data corruption, not an error that the ECC corrects.

Two consequences for SK-RAFT campaigns:

  • A design that reads a BRAM with DO_REG = 0 can take the wrong word of stage 3 after a freeze. The BRAM hold register pass (auxiliary_components/bram_hold_pass) protects against this. This example builds without the pass to show the effect.
  • TargetMemory.BRAM injection into a BRAM with EN_ECC_WRITE = TRUE does not test the built-in ECC. It gives a valid word with wrong data.

BscanPrimitive(user, length), dev.write_bscan(primitive, value), dev.read_bscan(primitive) Start and stop the clock (USER1), select the address (USER2), write the words and read the BRAM outputs (USER3).
dev.inject_at(far, word, bit, TargetMemory.BRAM) Stage 3: inject into word 0, bit 0. The script finds the location of the bit (Ram=B:BIT0) in the LL file.

Component injection: the components of a design, and random flip-flop upsets in one component¶

This example shows the components of the design hierarchy as a tree, with the number of flip-flops in each component. Then it injects upsets only into the flip-flops of one of these components, and the LEDs show the effect. It uses the design of example 2 (bscan_adder_top)

A component is one or more whole levels of the net paths in the LL file. For example, the net bscan_u1_operands/bscan_interface_read_write_uX/data_user_reg_data_in[2] is inside the component bscan_u1_operands. The last level, data_user_reg_data_in[2], is the net. It is not a component. A part of a name is not a component: bscan_u1 does not select this net.

Example of the hierarchy¶

Using bscan_adder_top as an example.

3 top-level components:

bscan_u1_operands (20 flip-flops)
`-- bscan_interface_read_write_uX (20 flip-flops)
bscan_u2_simplex_adder_res (5 flip-flops)
`-- bscan_interface_read_write_uX (5 flip-flops)
bscan_u3_tmr_adder_res (5 flip-flops)
`-- bscan_interface_read_write_uX (5 flip-flops)

Sequence¶

  1. The script uploads the bitstream and the LL file, and programs the FPGA. The server reads the LL file when it programs the FPGA. Thus, dev.components() needs a programmed design.
  2. Part 1. The script gets the components with dev.components(). The result is a list of the top-level components. Each component holds its sub components.
  3. The script prints each top-level component with print(component). This shows the component and all its sub components as a tree. Then the script prints the full path of each component, with its number of flip-flops.
  4. Part 2. The script finds COMPONENT (bscan_u1_operands) in the components. If the design has no such component, the script stops. If it has, the script prints the number of flip-flops in the component.
  5. The script injects one upset each 0.5 s with dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.FF, component=COMPONENT), until you press Enter. The server selects a random flip-flop of the component, also in its sub components.
  6. The script programs the FPGA again, to clear the upsets.

For each upset, the script prints the location of the flip-flop (FAR, word and bit) and the net that the flip-flop drives. The net is always inside COMPONENT.

The calls of the example¶

Call Use in the example
SkraftFpga.connect(ip=..., port=...), client.attach(SERIAL_NUMBER) Connect to the SK-RAFT server and attach to the device, in with statements that release the device and close the connection.
Design(bit, ll), dev.uploadDesignToServer(design), dev.programFPGA(design) Give the design files, upload them to the server and program the FPGA.
dev.configure_seed(0) Set the seed of the random injections. The same seed gives the same upsets in each run.
dev.components() Part 1: get the components of the design as a tree, with the number of flip-flops in each component.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.FF, component=COMPONENT) Part 2: inject one upset into a random flip-flop of one component. The report gives the net of the flip-flop (net_name).

Run the example¶

  1. Make sure that the design files are in hw/design_examples/<board>/bscan_adder_top/, and set BOARD in src/main.py to your board. Refer to Build a design or Prebuilt design files.
  2. At the top of src/main.py, set SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP and SERIAL_NUMBER. The design files are bscan_adder_top.bit and bscan_adder_top.ll. The script uploads them to the server.
  3. Run the script:
cd src
python main.py
Constant Default Description
COMPONENT "bscan_u1_operands" The full path of the component, as part 1 prints it.
INJECTION_PERIOD_S 0.5 The time between two upsets, in seconds.

Result¶

The script prints the tree, the full paths, and then one line for each upset: the number of the upset, the FAR, the word, the bit and the net. In targeted_top, the top-level components are clk_gen_inst (the clock generator), fast_heartbeat and slow_heartbeat.

The number of flip-flops and the locations depend on the build of your design. The numbers come from the LL file. If you exclude pblocks or frames, dev.inject_random() can select fewer flip-flops of a component than the tree shows. The script sets the seed (dev.configure_seed(0)). Thus, with the same design, each run injects into the same sequence of flip-flops.

If no flip-flop of the LL file is inside a component, the script prints a message and stops.

The script does not correct the upsets, and it does not stop the clock of the design during the injection. If your design must not run during the injection, stop its clock first, as example 3 does. At the end, the script programs the FPGA again to clear the upsets.

If you stop the script with Ctrl+C, the configuration of the device can stay incorrect. In that case, program the FPGA again before you do other work.

Hardware designs for the getting-started examples¶

This folder contains the Vivado build script, the VHDL sources and the constraint files of the getting-started examples. Each top-level design in sources_1/new/ shows a different part of the fault-injection setup: targeted CRAM injection (targeted_top), a comparison of two circuits (bscan_adder_top), and the application memory elements FF, LUTRAM and BRAM (ff_lut_top, brams_top, bram_readback_writeback_top). The scripts control the designs and read their results through JTAG/BSCAN. targeted_top shows its state on the LEDs only.

Designs¶

  • targeted_top: two independent heartbeat counters (slow and fast) for targeted fault-injection tests.
  • bscan_adder_top: two adders that BSCAN controls. One BSCAN write register (USER1) supplies the operands to a simplex adder and to a TMR adder. The script reads the result of the simplex adder through USER2 and the result of the TMR adder through USER3.
  • ff_lut_top: a flip-flop shift register that operates continuously, and a LUTRAM with an address map. The JTAG interface controls the clock of the shift register. BSCAN controls the two elements.
  • brams_top: one block RAM with a Hamming SEC code for each byte. Independent JTAG/BSCAN registers supply the address and the data.
  • bram_readback_writeback_top: one block RAM with the built-in ECC and no output register, for example4/readback_writeback. The read port is always enabled, and JTAG/BSCAN reads the BRAM outputs directly.

Each design is a full top-level design. The project has no default synthesis top.

Prebuilt designs¶

design_examples/design_examples.zip contains the prebuilt design files of the five designs for the Basys 3 (basys3) and the ZedBoard (zedboard). To extract them, run the script for your operating system:

cd design_examples
./unzip_designs.sh        # Linux
.\unzip_designs.bat       # Windows

The script extracts the files to design_examples/<board>/<top>/. For other boards, build the designs as described below.

Build a bitstream¶

The script create_project.tcl makes the Vivado project, sets one of the designs above as the synthesis top, and builds the bitstream. You must give only the board and the design. The script finds the XDC file of that board in xdc/<device>/<top>.xdc.

vivado -mode batch -source create_project.tcl -tclargs <device> <top> [project_name] [project_dir] [-gui]

Example:

vivado -mode batch -source create_project.tcl -tclargs basys3 brams_top

To open the project in the Vivado GUI after the build, add -gui at any position in the arguments. Vivado then stays open, and you can examine or change the project.

The script writes the bitstream to <project_dir>/<project_name>.runs/impl_1/<top>.bit. For targeted_top, bscan_adder_top, ff_lut_top, brams_top and bram_readback_writeback_top, the script also copies these files into design_examples/<device>/<top>/:

  • The bitstream.
  • The EBD and LL files, if Vivado makes them.
  • The XDC file, with the name board.xdc.

If this folder does not exist (for example, for your own board), the script creates it. Files from design_examples.zip in that folder are overwritten. Thus you can run the related example immediately after the build. Set BOARD in its main.py to the name of the board.

For brams_top, the script sets the BRAM hold register pass as the hook before opt_design (STEPS.OPT_DESIGN.TCL.PRE of impl_1). The pass is auxiliary_components/bram_hold_pass/bram_hold_hook.tcl at the root of the repository; the list tops_with_bram_hold in the script selects the tops. The pass writes bram_hold_pass.rpt in the impl_1 run directory, and the script prints it after the build. Refer to the pass README for what it changes and why.

The known devices are basys3 (Digilent Basys 3, xc7a35tcpg236-1) and zedboard (ZedBoard, xc7z020clg484-1). SolidKosmos tested and supplies only these two boards.

To add your own board:

  1. Copy the template folder: 
    cp -r xdc/custom_template xdc/<your_board_name>
  2. In each .xdc file of the new folder, replace the PACKAGE_PIN and IOSTANDARD placeholders. If you use pblocks, also replace the pblock ranges.
  3. In create_project.tcl, add an entry for <your_board_name> to device_info. Give only part and clk_freq. The script gets g_family from the Vivado ARCHITECTURE property of the part. For example: 
    my_board {part xc7a100tcsg324-1 clk_freq 100}
  4. Build the design with the name of your board, as for all other boards: 
    vivado -mode batch -source create_project.tcl -tclargs my_board brams_top

Device family (g_family generic)¶

Two wrappers have a g_family generic ("7SERIES", "ULTRASCALE" or "ULTRASCALEPLUS"). This generic selects the primitive that the wrapper uses:

  • bram_sdp_native_wrapper: RAMB36E1 or RAMB36E2.
  • clk_gen_wrapper: PLLE2_BASE, PLLE3_BASE or PLLE4_BASE.

create_project.tcl sets this generic for you. It reads the Vivado ARCHITECTURE property of the target part. Then it gives the related g_family value (and clk_freq) as a project generic, which replaces the default value in the VHDL. For a known device, you do not set this generic yourself. The script gets it from the part value of the device in device_info.

SK-RAFT cheat sheet¶

Short code snippets for the routines that you use most with the skraft Python client. For the rules of the injection setup, refer to general_guidelines.md. For each method and its parameters, refer to the Python API reference.

All snippets after the first one use dev, the device that client.attach() gives.

Connect and reserve a device¶

from skraft import SkraftFpga, SkraftError

with SkraftFpga.connect(ip="127.0.0.1", port=50051) as client:
    print(client.version())                      # server version
    for d in client.get_devices():               # connected boards
        print(d.serial_number, d.part_number)

    with client.attach("210183BFD452A") as dev:  # reserve one board
        dev.configure_seed(42)                   # repeatable random injections (set after attach)
        ...

With TLS (the server runs with -tls-cert and -tls-key):

client = SkraftFpga.connect(ip="10.0.0.5", port=50051,
                            tls_server_cert="server.crt",          # verify the server
                            tls_cert="client.crt", tls_key="client.key")  # only if the server checks the client

Upload and program a design¶

from skraft import Design

design = Design(bit="top.bit", ebd="top.ebd", ll="top.ll", xdc="top.xdc")
dev.uploadDesignToServer(design)   # the server keeps each uploaded design
dev.programFPGA(design)            # program again at any time to clear all upsets
Target Files that the design must have
TargetMemory.CRAM bit
TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM bit, ebd
TargetMemory.FF, LUTRAM, BRAM bit, ll
pblock= or exclude_pblock= also xdc
component= also ll

Count the bits¶

from skraft import TargetMemory

dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM)                  # whole design
dev.bit_count(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock="pb_tmr")  # one pblock
dev.all_bit_counts()                                         # dict with all counts

Inject into the CRAM and correct the upset¶

import time

report = dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM)
print(f"far {report.far:#010x} word {report.word_index} bit {report.bit_index}")
time.sleep(0.1)                                              # keep the upset
dev.inject_at(report.far, report.word_index, report.bit_index,
              TargetMemory.CRAM)                             # flip the bit back

Inject into a pblock, or exclude pblocks¶

dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock="pb_tmr")          # only inside pb_tmr
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM,
                  exclude_pblock={"harness_pblock"})                    # never inside the test harness

The exclusion applies to that call only. To list the pblocks of the XDC file, use dev.pblocks().

Inject into the flip-flops of a component¶

for component in dev.components():   # hierarchy from the LL file
    print(component)                 # tree with the flip-flop count of each component

dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.FF, component="top_component/sub_component")

component= works with TargetMemory.FF only. Stop the clock first (next section).

Inject into the application memory (FF, LUTRAM, BRAM)¶

Stop the clock of the design through BSCAN, inject, then start the clock again. The design must have the clock gate on USER1 (refer to auxiliary_components/bscan).

from skraft import BscanPrimitive

USER_CLK_EN = BscanPrimitive(1, 1)   # USER1, 1 bit: 1 = clock runs

def inject_frozen(dev, target, **options):
    dev.write_bscan(USER_CLK_EN, 0)          # stop the clock
    try:
        return dev.inject_random(target, **options)
    finally:
        dev.write_bscan(USER_CLK_EN, 1)      # start the clock, also if the injection fails

report = inject_frozen(dev, TargetMemory.FF, pblock="pb_sr")
report = inject_frozen(dev, TargetMemory.BRAM)

To revert the upset, flip the same bit with the clock stopped:

dev.write_bscan(USER_CLK_EN, 0)
dev.inject_at(report.far, report.word_index, report.bit_index, TargetMemory.BRAM)
dev.write_bscan(USER_CLK_EN, 1)

A BRAM port without an output register (DO_REG = 0) needs the BRAM hold register pass. Refer to general_guidelines.md.

Inject into one bit from the LL file¶

def ll_bit(ll_file, name):
    """FAR, word and bit of a BRAM bit, for example name="BIT0" (Ram=B:BIT0)."""
    with open(ll_file, encoding="ascii") as f:
        for line in f:
            fields = line.split()
            if fields[:1] == ["Bit"] and f"Ram=B:{name}" in fields:
                offset = int(fields[3])
                return int(fields[2], 16), offset // 32, offset % 32
    raise ValueError(f"Ram=B:{name} is not in {ll_file}")

far, word, bit = ll_bit("top.ll", "BIT0")
dev.inject_at(far, word, bit, TargetMemory.BRAM)    # with the clock stopped

Inject into every bit¶

reports, count = dev.inject_exhaustive(TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, pblock="pb_tmr")

Read and write BSCAN registers¶

from skraft import Bscan

USER_DATA = BscanPrimitive(3, 32)                         # USER3, 32 bits
dev.write_bscan(USER_DATA, 0x1234)
value = int.from_bytes(dev.read_bscan(USER_DATA), "big")  # bytes, MSB first

data = Bscan(dev, 3, 32)                                  # the same register, as integers
data.write(0x1234)
value = data.read()

Read back configuration frames¶

from skraft import ReadbackOption

frames = dev.readback(ReadbackOption.READBACK)            # all frames
frames = dev.readback(ReadbackOption.READBACK_CAPTURE)    # also the flip-flop values (stop the clock)
frames = dev.readback_range(0x00C00000, 0x00C0007F)       # a range, end included

frame = frames[0]
print(f"{frame.far:#010x}", [w.value for w in frame.words][:4])
print(dev.decode_far(frame.far).minor_address)            # block type, row, column, minor

The first and the last frame of a full readback are dummy frames, with the FAR of a real frame. Refer to readback_scrubbing.

Write a frame back (correct one frame)¶

golden = {}
for f in dev.readback(ReadbackOption.READBACK):
    golden.setdefault(f.far, f)  # keep the first frame of each FAR, not the dummy frame
...
dev.write_frame(golden[far])     # restore one frame from the golden copy

Exclude frames from injection¶

dev.exclude_frames([0x00400F9F, 0x00400FA0])   # the feature operations skip these frames; inject_at does not

Scrubbing and campaigns on the server¶

from skraft import ScrubbingType, FpgaFiSession, FaultType

report = dev.scrub(ScrubbingType.ESSENTIAL, scrub_cycle=1, duration_ms=10_000)
for cycle in report.scrub_summaries:
    print(cycle.scrub_cycle, len(cycle.word_summaries), "words differed from the golden data")

session = FpgaFiSession(fault_type=FaultType.RANDOM, duration_ms=10_000,
                        correction_time_ms=100, time_between_faults_ms=200,
                        sbu_percent=100.0, mbu_percent=0.0, mcu_percent=0.0,
                        target=TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM, correct=True)
summary = dev.run_campaign(session)
print(summary.faults_injected, summary.corrected)

The parameter values are only examples. Refer to scrub and run_campaign in the API reference.

Read the XADC sensors¶

from skraft import TEMPERATURE, VCCINT, TEMPERATURE_UPPER

dev.xadc(TEMPERATURE).value        # degC
dev.xadc(VCCINT).value             # V
dev.set_xadc_alarm(TEMPERATURE_UPPER, 85.0)
dev.xadc_flags().temperature       # True while the temperature alarm is on

Read a configuration register¶

from skraft import RegisterAddress

status = dev.read_register(RegisterAddress.STATUS)

Handle errors and leave a clean device¶

try:
    ...
except SkraftError as e:          # base class of all client errors
    print(f"failed: {e}")
finally:
    dev.programFPGA(design)       # clear all upsets before other work

SK-RAFT concepts¶

For the rules of the injection setup (safe-startup clock, clock stop during application memory injection, BRAM output latch), refer to general_guidelines.md. For code snippets, refer to cheatsheet.md.

Conceptual model of an SRAM-based FPGA¶

The following figure presents a conceptual model of an SRAM-based FPGA to illustrate the radiation-induced failure modes of such devices. The model divides the chip into two layers: the configuration layer, which holds the FPGA's configuration memory (CRAM), and the application layer, which implements the circuit. A failure in the application layer can arise for two reasons. First, highly energetic particles, such as heavy ions, can strike and corrupt the CRAM bits that configure the resources the circuit uses, thereby altering the logic or routing of the implemented design. Second, particles can strike and corrupt application memory elements in the application layer (ARAM), such as flip-flops and the contents of block RAMs (BRAMs).

Each fault that SK-RAFT injects goes into one of the two layers:

  • CRAM layer: Corrupts the FPGA's programmable resources, such as LUTs, global and local routing, and BRAM mode and width. A fault (i.e., a bit flip) in this layer changes the structure of the application circuit. The directives TargetMemory.CRAM and TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM inject faults into the configuration layer.
  • ARAM layer: Corrupts the dynamic state of the configured circuit during operation. Examples include the current value of a flip-flop and the data in a BRAM or a LUTRAM. A fault in this layer changes a value but not the circuit. Directives TargetMemory.FF, TargetMemory.LUTRAM and TargetMemory.BRAM inject into the application layer.

Targeted fault injection¶

Essential bits¶

Even the densest FPGA design uses only a small part of the CRAM. Thus, a bit flip (fault) in CRAM (TargetMemory.CRAM) usually goes into one of these unused CRAM bits. Then the flip has no effect that you can see.

Essential bits are CRAM bits that, when corrupted, can cause an application-observable error. SK-RAFT reads the bits from the .ebd file of the design that is generated from Vivado bitgen. Thus, targeting faults only in essential CRAM bits (TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM) can significantly reduce testing time, since only those bits that matter are tested.

Targeting or excluding resources from fault injection¶

You can inject faults only to the resources of a specific Pblock defined in your XDC constraints file. Combine pblock=<pblock_name> with TargetMemory.FF, TargetMemory.LUTRAM, TargetMemory.BRAM, TargetMemory.CRAM and TargetMemory.ESSENTIAL_CRAM to inject faults into the specific Pblock. To exclude configuration frames from testing, give their frame addresses (FARs) to dev.exclude_frames(). The exclusion has no effect on dev.inject_at().

Location of a bit: FAR, word index and bit index¶

SK-RAFT always uses three coordinates for the location of a bit, in reports and in arguments:

  1. The frame address (FAR).
  2. The word index in the frame.
  3. The bit index in the word.

dev.decode_far() decodes a FAR into its block type, top or bottom half, row, column and minor frame number (see 7 Series FPGAs Configuration User Guide - UG470).

SK-RAFT injection setup: general guidelines¶

The rules that a design must obey for correct fault injection with SK-RAFT, and the reasons for them. For the general concepts (CRAM, ARAM, essential bits), refer to concepts.md. For code snippets of the common routines, refer to cheatsheet.md.

1. Use a safe-startup clock source¶

Rule: The source of each clock tree in the design must be a PLL or an MMCM with safe startup. The output clock must stay off until the PLL has locked.

Why: An experiment can program the FPGA again many times, for example to remove the upsets of one step before the next step. After each programming, the design starts again. Without safe startup, the design can run on the clock while the PLL is not stable, and start in an incorrect state. Then a failure that the script sees can come from the startup, and not from the injected fault.

In this repository:

  • auxiliary_components/safe_clk_gen/: clk_gen_wrapper, a PLL for 7-series, UltraScale and UltraScale+. It enables the output BUFGCE only after LOCKED has passed an 8-stage shift register.
  • targeted_top, ff_lut_top, brams_top and bram_readback_writeback_top (in get_started/hw/sources_1/new/), test_neo_hardened, sem_arbitration and mmcm_drp_interface use clk_gen_wrapper.
  • All the examples program the FPGA at the start, and some examples program it again between their steps (for example example1 and example4).

2. Stop the clock during application memory injection¶

Rule: Before an injection into the application memory (TargetMemory.FF, TargetMemory.LUTRAM or TargetMemory.BRAM), stop the clock of the logic that uses that memory. Start the clock again after the injection.

Why: SK-RAFT gets access to the application memory through the configuration interface (readback, frame write, and capture of the flip-flop states). These operations are asynchronous to the application clock and change the application memory directly. If the clock runs during the access, the design can sample data that is not stable.

dev.write_bscan(USER_CLK_EN, 0)         # stop the clock
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.FF)      # inject
dev.write_bscan(USER_CLK_EN, 1)         # start the clock

In this repository:

  • auxiliary_components/bscan/README.md: the clock gate. A BSCAN USER register (USER1) drives the CE of a BUFGCE. The README has the VHDL, the XDC and the Python calls.
  • auxiliary_components/README.md: the full sequence (stop, inject, start, read the result).
  • example3 (flip-flops and LUTRAM) and example4 (BRAM) stop the clock with USER1 for each injection.

AMD references:

  • XAPP1230 (v1.1), Configuration Readback Capture in UltraScale FPGAs: "the user must stop the clocks with the associated logic to freeze the user state". For 7-series: "Xilinx recommends stopping the clock of the associated user logic while the GCAPTURE command is being loaded".
  • UG470, 7 Series FPGAs Configuration User Guide, Chapter 6, "Readback Capture" (GCAPTURE and the CAPTUREE2 primitive).
  • UG570 (v1.17), UltraScale Architecture Configuration User Guide, Chapter 10, "Readback Capture" (pp. 193-194): "In the UltraScale FPGAs, you must stop or disable the clock associated with the user state elements being targeted throughout the duration of the readback capture sequence."
  • UG953, Vivado Design Suite 7 Series FPGA and Zynq 7000 SoC Libraries Guide, CAPTUREE2: only flip-flop and latch states can be captured. LUTRAM, SRL and block RAM states can be read back, but not captured.

3. BRAM injection changes the BRAM output¶

Rule: For each BRAM port without an output register (DO_REG = 0), add a hold register behind the output. Use the BRAM hold register pass to add it.

Why: Each SK-RAFT access to a BRAM content frame (readback, inject and revert) changes the output latch of the BRAMs in that frame. The value on DO changes, but the stored content and the FIFO pointers do not change. If the design uses DO after the clock starts again, it gets the changed value and not the word that it read before the freeze. Ports with the output register (DO_REG = 1) keep the word while the clock is stopped, and do not need the hold register.

The pass works only if the design obeys these requirements:

  1. The clock gate stops the clock low. Use a BUFGCE, not a BUFGCE_1.
  2. The half-cycle paths to and from the hold register meet timing.
  3. SK-RAFT injects only while the clock is stopped (rule 2).
  4. The XDC excludes the BRAMs from power optimization:
set_power_opt -exclude_cells [get_cells -hier -filter {REF_NAME =~ RAMB*}]

In this repository:

  • auxiliary_components/bram_hold_pass/README.md: the problem, the hold register, the requirements and the report of the pass.
  • example4/readback_writeback: shows the effect. The BRAM outputs a wrong word while the clock is stopped after an injection.
  • example4: a BRAM protected by the pass.
  • get_started/hw/create_project.tcl (list tops_with_bram_hold) and application_examples/test_neo_hardened/create_project.tcl set the pass as the hook before opt_design.

AMD references:

  • UG570 (v1.17), UltraScale Architecture Configuration User Guide, Chapter 10, "SEU Detection and Correction" (p. 192): "Block RAM content is skipped during readback to avoid interfering with user functions." The guide does not describe the effect on the output latch. The effect above comes from the measurements of example4/readback_writeback.

MMCM dynamic reconfiguration: the client script changes the MMCM clocks over BSCAN¶

This example shows how to change the output clocks of an MMCM while the design runs. The client script sends Dynamic Reconfiguration Port (DRP) accesses to the FPGA through a BSCAN register, and a small state machine in the design does each access on the DRP of the MMCM. The script reads and writes the MMCM registers in the sequence of XAPP888, and the effect shows on two LEDs: each MMCM output clock drives a heartbeat.

Tested on¶

Board Device
Digilent Basys 3 Artix-7 xc7a35tcpg236-1

The MMCM wrapper supports 7 series (MMCME2_ADV), UltraScale (MMCME3_ADV) and UltraScale+ (MMCME4_ADV): the g_family generic selects the primitive. For another board, change the part, g_family and the XDC file in create_project.tcl. The DRP addresses in main.py are the 7-series addresses (XAPP888); on UltraScale, the power register is 0x27.

Files¶

File Description
src/main.py The test script: the DRP accesses over BSCAN, the XAPP888 reconfiguration sequence, the stages.
create_project.tcl Creates the Vivado project with the sources and the constraints, and builds the bitstream.
hw/src/mmcm_drp_interface_top.vhd The top: the safe clock, BSCAN USER1, the DRP control FSM, the MMCM and the two heartbeats.
hw/src/DRP_control.vhd The DRP control FSM: one DRP access for each packet, the MMCM reset and the watchdog.
hw/src/mmcm_wrapper.vhd The MMCM with all ports, for 7 series, UltraScale and UltraScale+.
hw/src/heartbeat.vhd A counter that toggles its output every 10,000,000 clock cycles.
hw/xdc/basys3.xdc Pins, clocks and bitstream settings.
images/ The block diagram.

The build adds the BSCAN interface and the safe-startup PLL from auxiliary_components/.

BSCAN register¶

Register Write (32 bits) Read (24 bits)
USER1 The DRP packet. Bits 31:25: padding. Bit 24: MMCM RST. Bit 23: 1 = write, 0 = read. Bits 22:16: DRP address. Bits 15:0: DRP write data. Bits 23:17: the current DRP address. Bits 16:1: the DO of the MMCM. Bit 0: the DRP error (watchdog timeout).

The length of each direction is a whole number of bytes. The write has 7 padding bits for this reason.

On the Basys 3, LD0 shows the heartbeat of CLKOUT0 (led_o[0]) and LD1 the heartbeat of CLKOUT1 (led_o[1]).

How the DRP control works¶

Each BSCAN write is one packet. On the rising edge of the BSCAN avail signal, the design moves the packet to the safe clock domain and gives the FSM a one-cycle command:

  1. If bit 24 (RST) is 1, the FSM asserts RST of the MMCM and does one DRP access: DEN for one clock cycle, DWE = bit 23, with the address and the data of the packet. Then it waits for DRDY.
  2. RST stays asserted between packets. A packet with bit 24 = 0 does no DRP access: it releases RST, and the MMCM locks again.
  3. If DRDY does not come within 1023 clock cycles, the FSM sets the error bit and keeps RST asserted. The script then decides what to do. The next successful access clears the error bit.

The DO of the MMCM goes directly to the BSCAN read register. The script reads it after each read packet.

How a reconfiguration works¶

The script changes the MMCM in the sequence of XAPP888:

  1. Write the power register (0x28) with 0xFFFF. This first packet also asserts RST.
  2. For each register to change: read it, keep the bits outside the field, set the field, write it, and read it back to check it.
  3. Release RST (a packet with bit 24 = 0) and wait 100 ms for the lock.

The registers of each output are ClkReg1 (PHASE MUX, HIGH TIME, LOW TIME) and ClkReg2 (MX, EDGE, NO COUNT, DELAY TIME, and the fractional bits of CLKOUT0). For an integer divide D with a 50 % duty cycle, HIGH TIME = D / 2 (rounded down), LOW TIME = D - HIGH TIME and EDGE = D mod 2. The VCO frequency does not change in this example, so the lock and filter registers stay as they are.

Output ClkReg1 ClkReg2
CLKOUT0 0x08 0x09
CLKOUT1 0x0A 0x0B

The stages¶

The MMCM starts with a VCO of 1000 MHz (M = 10, D = 1) and CLKOUT0 and CLKOUT1 at 1000 MHz / 10 = 100 MHz. Each heartbeat toggles every 10,000,000 cycles of its clock. The script waits for Enter before each stage.

# Change Result on the LEDs
0 Program the FPGA. Both LEDs toggle every 100 ms, together.
1 CLKOUT0 and CLKOUT1 divide 10 -> 50 (20 MHz), in one reconfiguration. Both LEDs toggle every 0.5 s, together.
2 CLKOUT1 divide 100 (10 MHz) for 1 s, then 50 again. The CLKOUT1 heartbeat falls 0.5 s behind, half of its 1 s blink period. The two LEDs blink in alternation.

Stage 2 does not change the phase of the clock. It changes the offset between the two heartbeat counters. A phase shift of the MMCM moves a clock by less than one clock period (for example, 25 ns for 90 degrees at 10 MHz), so it does not show on LEDs that toggle every 0.5 s. main.py has the functions for a phase change (phase_changes, phase_fields) for a test with an oscilloscope.

Requirements¶

  • SK-RAFT server, with the board connected through JTAG.
  • Vivado 2025.2 (the version that the Tcl script was written for) to build the design.
  • Python 3.9 or a later version, with the skraft package (api/python).

Generate the design¶

  1. Open the Vivado Tcl shell and run the script:
vivado -mode batch -source create_project.tcl

The script creates the project mmcm_drp_interface/mmcm_drp_interface.xpr next to itself and builds the bitstream. 2. The .bit file goes to mmcm_drp_interface/mmcm_drp_interface.runs/impl_1/. main.py reads it from there.

Run the example¶

  1. At the top of src/main.py, set SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP and SERIAL_NUMBER.
  2. Run the script:
python src/main.py
Constant Default Description
SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP / SK_RAFT_SERVER_PORT "127.0.0.1" / 50051 The address of the SK-RAFT server.
SERIAL_NUMBER "210183BFD452A" The serial number of the board. get_devices() gives the connected boards.
SLOW_DIVIDE 50 The divide of CLKOUT0 and CLKOUT1 in stage 1.
LAG_DIVIDE / LAG_TIME_S 100 / 1.0 The divide of CLKOUT1 in stage 2, and the time it runs at that divide, in seconds.

References¶

  • XAPP888, MMCM and PLL Dynamic Reconfiguration: the bit fields and the DRP addresses of the MMCM registers, and the reconfiguration sequence.

Readback scrubbing in Python¶

This example corrects upsets in the configuration memory (CRAM) of the FPGA with a readback scrubber that runs on the client. The script uses only the readback and the frame write of SK-RAFT. It does not use the scrubbing of the server (dev.scrub()). Thus you can see each step of the scrubber, and change it.

The script does not need design files, and it does not program the FPGA. It scrubs the design that is in the FPGA.

To show the scrubber at work, the script injects one random upset into the CRAM before each scrub cycle. The upset stays in the CRAM until the next scrub cycle.

The output has this form (the values are only an example):

Device: serial number 210183BFD452A, part number XC7A35T
Golden frames: 5568, checked frames: 5542
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cycle  1: 1 upset(s) corrected | correction 0.012 s | cycle 2.100 s | idle 5.000 s
    far 0x00401f00 word  12 bit  7 (golden 0x00000000, read 0x00000080)
    injected far 0x00401f00 word  12 bit  7: corrected

How the scrubber works¶

  1. At the start, the script reads back all the frames of the CRAM. These frames are the golden frames.
  2. In each scrub cycle, the script reads back all the frames again, and compares each frame with its golden frame.
  3. For each frame that is different, the script writes the golden frame back, at its frame address (FAR).

The script does not check these frames:

Frames Why
Dummy (pad) frames The first and the last frame of a readback, and each frame with the same FAR as the frame before it. A dummy frame does not hold configuration data. Its FAR is the FAR of a real frame, thus a write would change the real frame.
BRAM content frames (block type 1) The contents of the BRAMs change during operation.

The SK-RAFT scrubber on the server does the same steps. The script is different in these points:

  • The golden frames come from the readback at the start of the script. If an upset is in the CRAM before this readback, the scrubber does not correct it.
  • The script does not tell essential upsets from non-essential upsets.

The calls of the example¶

Call Use in the example
dev.readback(ReadbackOption.READBACK) Read back all the frames of the CRAM, for the golden frames and in each scrub cycle.
dev.write_frame(frame) Write a golden frame back, at its frame address.
dev.decode_far(far) Get the block type of a frame. The script decodes only the frames that it needs, and keeps the result.
dev.configure_seed(seed) Set the seed of the random injections. The same seed gives the same upsets in each run.
dev.inject_random(TargetMemory.CRAM) Inject one upset into a random bit of the CRAM. The server does not inject into the dummy frames, and into the frames that it excludes, for example the frames of the IOBs.
dev.inject_at(far, word, bit, TargetMemory.CRAM) Flip an injected bit again, if it is in a BRAM content frame. Then the script injects again.

Requirements¶

  • SK-RAFT server, with the FPGA board connected through JTAG. The server must support the frame write (FpgaWriteFrame).
  • Python 3.9 or a later version, with the skraft package installed (api/python).

Run the example¶

  1. At the top of src/main.py, set SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP and SERIAL_NUMBER.
  2. Run the script:
cd src
python main.py
Constant Default Description
SK_RAFT_SERVER_IP / SK_RAFT_SERVER_PORT "127.0.0.1" / 50051 The address of the SK-RAFT server.
SERIAL_NUMBER "210183BFD452A" The serial number of the target board. get_devices() gives the connected boards.
SCRUB_CYCLES 10 The number of scrub cycles.
SCRUB_PERIOD_S 5.0 The time from the start of one scrub cycle to the start of the next, in seconds.
INJECT_UPSETS True If True, the script injects one upset before each scrub cycle.
SEED 42 The seed of the random injections.

Result¶

In each cycle, the script shows the corrected bits, and if it corrected the injected bit. The script also shows:

Value Meaning
correction The time of the frame writes of the cycle.
cycle The time of the full scrub cycle: the readback, the comparison and the frame writes.
idle The time from the end of the previous cycle (or of the golden readback) to the start of this cycle.

Each cycle also shows that the correction of the previous cycle operated: if a write did not correct a bit, the next cycle shows the bit again.

Troubleshooting¶

Problem Cause Solution
The script corrects upsets in each cycle, also with INJECT_UPSETS = False The design in the FPGA has configuration bits that change during operation, for example LUTRAM or SRL bits. The script compares all the bits of the checked frames. Use a design that does not have these bits.
failed to write frame ...: unknown method FpgaWriteFrame ... The SK-RAFT server is older than the client, and does not support the frame write. Update the SK-RAFT server.

SEM arbitration: SK-RAFT injects, the SEM corrects¶

This example shows how SK-RAFT and the Soft Error Mitigation (SEM) controller of the FPGA can share the configuration logic. SK-RAFT injects upsets into the configuration memory (CRAM) while the SEM is idle. Then the SEM scans the CRAM again and reports what it finds on the UART of the board. The script compares the reports of the SEM with the injected bits (output of experiment 1, shortened):

SEM status after I: idle
clock off
injected far 00020518 (block type 0) word  50 bit  0
clock on
> O
  SEM| SC 04
  SEM| SED OK
  SEM| PA 00020518
  SEM| WD 32 BT 00
  SEM| COR
  ...
    FAR       WORD  BIT  REPORTED
    00020518    50    0  yes, PA 00020518
The SEM reported 1 of 1 injected bits.

The lines that start with SEM| are the UART text of the SEM.
